title: Who Owns Your Listing Photos When You Leave a Brokerage?
metaDesc: Paying the photographer does not transfer copyright. Under federal law it stays with them unless you have a signed agreement. Your portfolio may not be yours.
h1: Who Owns Your Listing Photos When You Leave a Brokerage?
about: Who holds copyright in real estate listing photography under federal law, why paying the invoice does not transfer ownership, what the MLS license actually covers, what the Ninth Circuit held in VHT v. Zillow about license scope, and what a Florida agent should settle in writing before a shoot.
answer: Usually not you, and often not your brokerage either. Under federal copyright law the photographer owns the images unless they were your employee shooting within the scope of that employment, or you signed a written work-made-for-hire agreement and the work fits one of nine narrow categories. Paying the invoice buys you a license, not the copyright. What you carry to a new brokerage is therefore a question about the scope of that license, and the scope is usually tied to marketing the property for sale. Your portfolio, your just-sold posts and your listing presentation all sit outside that purpose.
takeaways: Copyright vests in the photographer at the moment of the shot. Paying for the shoot does not move it.

Under 17 U.S.C. 101 a commissioned work is a work made for hire only if the parties expressly agreed in writing and the work falls in one of nine enumerated categories. Photographs do not automatically qualify.
What you normally receive is a license, and a license has a purpose. Listing photography is typically licensed in relation to the sale of that property.

In VHT, Inc. v. Zillow Group, Inc., 918 F.3d 723 (9th Cir. 2019), the Ninth Circuit held the defendant platform liable for direct infringement on uses that went beyond the license purpose, and rejected fair use because making photographs searchable was not transformative.

The whole problem is solved by one paragraph agreed before the shoot. After the shoot you are negotiating from a weaker position, and after you have left the brokerage you may have no position at all.
tldr: Listing photographs almost never belong to the agent. Federal law leaves copyright with the photographer unless there is an employment relationship or a signed work-made-for-hire agreement covering a qualifying category, and photographs rarely qualify. What an agent holds is a license granted for a purpose, usually marketing that property for sale, which is why a portfolio built from past listings is legally shakier than it feels. The fix is a written grant agreed before the camera comes out.
body:
This one surprises people because the money makes it feel settled. You chose the photographer, you scheduled the shoot, you paid the invoice, the images are of a house you listed. It reads like ownership. It is not.

The question matters most at exactly the moment an agent stops thinking about it, which is when they change brokerages and want to take a body of work with them.

The default rule, and it is not intuitive

Copyright in a photograph belongs to the person who took it, from the moment the shutter closes. Nothing about paying for the work changes that on its own. The only routes to someone else owning it are an employment relationship, a written transfer, or the work-made-for-hire doctrine, and that last one is much narrower than its name suggests.

Under 17 U.S.C. 101, a work qualifies as made for hire in exactly two ways. The first is a work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment. The second is a specially ordered or commissioned work where the parties expressly agreed in writing that it is a work made for hire, and the work falls within one of nine enumerated categories: a contribution to a collective work, part of a motion picture or audiovisual work, a translation, a supplementary work, a compilation, an instructional text, a test, answer material for a test, or an atlas.

The Copyright Office states the consequence directly: a work prepared by an independent contractor is not a work made for hire unless the parties have expressly agreed in writing that the work shall be a work made for hire. Absent that writing, copyright vests in the contractor.

Almost every real estate photographer is an independent contractor. Almost none of the shoots have that signed writing. And a set of listing photos does not obviously land in any of the nine categories, though people sometimes argue it is a contribution to a collective work. Two conditions, both usually unmet.

So what do you actually hold?

A license. Permission to use the images for a purpose, granted by the person who still owns them.

That word purpose is doing enormous work. A license granted for marketing a property for sale authorizes exactly that. It does not automatically authorize a portfolio page, a listing presentation shown to a future seller, an anniversary post, a paid advertisement for your personal brand, or the same images carried into a competing brokerage after you leave.

None of these are exotic hypotheticals. They are what a producing agent does with photographs every week.

The case that made scope a real issue

In VHT, Inc. v. Zillow Group, Inc., 918 F.3d 723 (9th Cir. 2019), a real estate photography company sued a national listing platform over its use of tens of thousands of images. The core of the dispute was not whether the photographs were licensed at all. It was whether the defendant had exceeded the scope of licenses that authorized use in relation to the sale of the property.

The outcome was mixed and the reasoning is the useful part. On the searchable, arranged and catalogued portion of the platform, the Ninth Circuit found direct infringement, rejecting the argument that the defendant was simply behaving like a search engine. It also rejected fair use, holding that making photographs searchable was not transformative.

An agent is not a national platform, and nobody is suggesting a portfolio page carries the same exposure as fifty thousand images. The transferable point is narrower and more useful: a court looked at a real estate photo license, asked what purpose it was granted for, and treated use beyond that purpose as infringement rather than as a technicality.

Where the brokerage sits in this

There are three common arrangements, and agents frequently do not know which one they are in:

  • The brokerage commissions and pays. The license typically runs to the brokerage. You had use of it while you were there. When you leave, you are asking your former firm for permission, and how that conversation goes usually depends on how the exit went.
  • You commission and pay personally. The license runs to you, which is better, but it is still a license with a purpose and you still do not own the copyright.
  • The seller commissioned the photography. Less common, and it makes the position weaker again, because your permission may be derivative of theirs.

This is a genuine infrastructure question, in the same family as who provides your signs and who installs them and the rest of what a brokerage actually provides. It is worth asking before joining, not after producing two years of listings.

It behaves like the rest of your book

The pattern here is the one that governs almost everything an agent accumulates inside a firm. Relationships travel. Paperwork and licensed assets generally do not. That is the same distinction that decides how portable your book of business is, and it is why a team member leaving and taking clients is such a reliably ugly conversation.

Photographs simply make it concrete, because you can point at the file and it still is not yours.

The fix, which is boring and takes one paragraph

Settle it before the shoot, in writing, with the photographer. Two workable versions:

  • An assignment. The photographer transfers copyright to you. Costs more, and many photographers will decline because their back catalogue is their business.
  • A broad license. Copyright stays with them, but the grant names the uses you actually need: marketing the property, your portfolio, your future listing presentations, your social and paid promotion, and continued use if you change brokerages. This is the realistic option and most photographers will price it reasonably if you ask up front.

Ask the same question of drone footage. If you are hiring a pilot rather than flying yourself, the same copyright analysis applies to the video, which is a wrinkle the Part 107 licensing question does not touch, because certification and copyright are two different subjects.

What to do about photographs you already have

Three practical moves, in order of usefulness:

  • Find out who commissioned each set. If the brokerage did, your permission likely came from them.
  • Ask the photographer directly for a portfolio license on past work. It is a small ask, it usually costs little or nothing, and photographers are used to the request.
  • For anything you cannot clear, use exterior shots you took yourself, or describe the work in text. Given how much professional photography matters to a listing, it is worth the small cost of clearing the images properly rather than quietly hoping.

The short version

You paid for the photographs and you do not own them. You hold a license, that license was granted for a purpose, and marketing your own career after you have left is a different purpose. One paragraph before the shoot settles it permanently, and it is far cheaper than the alternative.

The same license-and-ownership question applies to the other asset you built inside the firm: who owns your client database when you leave a brokerage.

faq.q: I paid the photographer. Why are the photos not mine?
faq.a: Because payment buys a license, not copyright. Under federal law copyright vests in the photographer at creation and moves only through an employment relationship, a written transfer, or a work-made-for-hire agreement. Paying an invoice is none of those three.

faq.q: What is a work made for hire?
faq.a: Under 17 U.S.C. 101 it is either a work prepared by an employee within the scope of employment, or a specially ordered or commissioned work where the parties expressly agreed in writing that it is a work made for hire and the work falls within one of nine enumerated categories. Absent that signed writing, a work prepared by an independent contractor is not a work made for hire and copyright stays with the contractor.

faq.q: Can I keep my listing photos in my portfolio after I change brokerages?
faq.a: It depends entirely on the scope of the license and on who commissioned the shoot. A license granted for marketing a property for sale does not obviously cover promoting your own career at a different firm. If the brokerage commissioned the photography, your permission likely ran through the brokerage. The safe route is to ask the photographer for a portfolio license, which is usually inexpensive.

faq.q: What did VHT, Inc. v. Zillow Group, Inc. decide?
faq.a: In that 2019 Ninth Circuit case, 918 F.3d 723, the court examined whether a national listing platform had exceeded the scope of licenses authorizing use of real estate photographs in relation to the sale of the property. It found direct infringement on the arranged and searchable portion of the site, rejected the search engine analogy, and rejected fair use on the ground that making photographs searchable was not transformative.

faq.q: What should I put in writing before a shoot?
faq.a: Either an assignment of copyright, or a license that names every use you actually need: marketing the property, your portfolio, future listing presentations, social and paid promotion, and continued use if you change brokerages. Agree it before the shoot. Afterwards you are negotiating from a weaker position, and after you have left the firm you may have none.

ctaHeading: Ask who owns the photography before you produce two years of it.
